sentences.text: She was not enormous and she was not small and she did not, when he finally got a proper look at her, seem in the least surprised.
She had come out and stopped about half a metre from his knee and turned herself broadside on, which he later learned is what they do when they are considering the situation rather than fleeing it.
She was not what he had pictured, which was a Christmas card.

She was bigger than a Christmas card and much dirtier, and there was a patch on her left side where the spines were thin, and she smelled — this is the detail he always includes and people never like — she smelled strongly of a hedge.
They looked at each other for a while.
A dog barked over towards the depot and neither of them reacted to it.

Rui said, "This is mine." The hedgehog did not say anything, because hedgehogs do not, and Rui would like that understood at the outset because people always assume this story has a talking animal in it and it does not.
What she did was go back under the hedge and come out again with something in her mouth.
It was another one.
Flat, about postcard size, with a dark blue evening in it and a smell of frost coming off it that he could feel on his face from where he sat.
It was not from the box.
That was the thing he understood immediately and could not have explained.
The box was on his knees with the lid on.

She had gone back under the hedge and had come out with a twelfth one from somewhere else, and he never found out where, and he did ask, later, in the only way available to him, which was to look under the hedge with a torch for about an hour.
She put it down on the ground in front of him, and then pushed it towards him with her nose, twice, in a way that could not have meant anything else.
He picked it up.
And that is how Rui found out what the last hour of a day feels like when it is handed back to you all at once instead of being lived through a minute at a time.
It was the eighth of October.
He knew it was the eighth of October because he was in it.

He was standing at the back door — the same back door — and the sky was that colour, and inside the house behind him his grandmother's carers were in the hall talking to his mother in the low voices that adults use when they think they are being quiet.

And Rui, standing at the back door on the eighth of October, was eleven years old and was not going to cry, and had gone out into the cold specifically so that he would not, and was doing the thing where you press your thumbnail hard into your finger.
The hour ran through him and finished and he was back in the mud in December with a piece of cardboard in his hand that was no longer anything at all.
It had lasted, by the clock, no time whatsoever.
He checked.
He had gone in and it had been twenty to five and he came out of it and it was twenty to five, and the light at the bottom of the yard had not changed.
It had also lasted an hour and ten minutes, all of it, in order, including the part in the middle where nothing happened and he had just stood there being cold.
He looked at the hedgehog.
The hedgehog looked back at him with the total lack of embarrassment of a creature that has done nothing wrong.
